1 OurBigBook.com
For the same massless spring of spring constant k, Hooke's law gives the vertical simple harmonic motion about the displaced equilibrium position:
νi​=2π1​mi​k​​,R=m2​m1​​=(ν1​ν2​​)2.
(1)
Gravity shifts the equilibrium extension but does not change this frequency. Use the measured sample means in the ratio estimate. For small measurement errors, logarithmic differentiation gives
RdR​=2ν2​dν2​​−2ν1​dν1​​.
(2)
Assuming the two frequency estimates have independent errors, their variances add. Writing ϵ=δν/ν for their common fractional standard uncertainty, monomial uncertainty propagation yields
(Rσ(R)​)2≃4ϵ2+4ϵ2,Rσ(R)​≃8​νδν​.​
(3)
This is a first-order uncertainty formula, rather than an exact identity for an arbitrary noisy ratio. It assumes that errors in the two measured frequencies have zero covariance.
There is a statistical distinction in the wording: the standard deviation of individual repetitions is not the standard error of their sample mean. If the supplied σ(νi​) describes individual trials, the frequency means have errors σ(νi​)/n​, and the ratio formed from those means instead satisfies
Rmeans​σ(Rmeans​)​≃n8​​νδν​.​
(4)
Thus the printed formula describes either a single-pair ratio or a convention in which δν already denotes the uncertainty of each averaged frequency. Under either consistent interpretation, independent repeated measurements reduce statistical error in proportion to n−1/2. Halving it requires 4n trials in total for each mass, or 3n additional trials. Repetition alone does not reduce a fixed systematic error.

The spacecraft clock measures proper time τ, while a clock at rest with Earth measures the launch-to-emission interval t. Neglect Earth's subsequent motion and gravity, as in the intended special relativity model. The Lorentz factor and time dilation give
γ=1−v2/c2​1​=8​3​,t=γτ=8​3​(12h)=12.7279h.
(5)
In Earth's inertial frame, the spacecraft's displacement at emission is d=vt. Therefore
d=8​cτ​=4.24264 light-hours≃4.58×1012m.​
(6)
Here τ=43200s and the speed of light is c=2.99792458×108ms−1. The distance is evaluated at the emission event, using simultaneous Earth-frame endpoints, as required by relativity of simultaneity; the return signal has not yet reached Earth. A distance assigned on the spacecraft's simultaneous time slice is different: Earth has moved away at c/3 for 12h in that frame, giving cτ/3=4 light-hours. Specifying the reference frame is essential to the numerical answer.

Use dimensions M,L,T for mass, length and time. The reduced Planck constant, gravitational constant and speed of light have dimensions
[ℏ]=ML2T−1,[G]=L3M−1T−2,[c]=LT−1.
(7)
For lp​=ℏαGβcγ to have the dimensions of a length, dimensional analysis requires
α−β=0,2α+3β+γ=1,−α−2β−γ=0.
(8)
The first equation gives β=α; the third gives γ=−3α. Substitution in the second gives 2α=1. Hence
α=21​,β=21​,γ=−23​,lp​=c3ℏG​​.​
(9)
With ℏ=1.054571817×10−34Js, G=6.67430×10−11m3kg−1s−2 and c=2.99792458×108ms−1, the Planck length is
lp​≃1.6163×10−35m.​
(10)
The proposed monomial fixes the dimensionless prefactor to one; dimensional analysis on its own cannot select an arbitrary dimensionless multiplier.

4 OurBigBook.com
First intensity minimum. In Fraunhofer diffraction, the path difference between adjacent slits is dsinθ, so the relative wave phase is δ=2πdsinθ/λ1​. Summing the N equal complex amplitudes as a geometric series gives the diffraction grating interference factor
I(θ)∝​∑j=0N−1​eijδ​2=sin2(δ/2)sin2(Nδ/2)​.
(11)
The central maximum has δ=0. Its nearest zero occurs at Nδ/2=π, where the denominator is nonzero. Thus
sinθmin​=Ndλ1​​=10(80×10−6)640×10−9​=8.00×10−4,∣θmin​∣=8.00×10−4rad=0.0458∘.​
(12)
There is a symmetric first zero on each side of the incident direction. The narrow slits are treated as having a sufficiently broad single-slit diffraction envelope.
Wavelength resolution and the missing order specification. Adopt the Rayleigh criterion: the principal maximum of one wavelength lies at the adjacent minimum of the other in the same nonzero diffraction order m. For λ2​>λ1​ and m>0, those directions obey
dsinθ=mλ2​=(m+N1​)λ1​.
(13)
Consequently the ideal resolving power of a diffraction grating is λ1​/Δλ=mN, giving
Δλmin,m​=mNλ1​​=m64​nm.​
(14)
The usual first-order reading therefore gives 64nm. Zero diffraction order cannot separate the two wavelengths, because both central maxima coincide.
The paper does not specify which diffraction order is observed, so 64nm is not an order-independent minimum. In the ideal infinitely narrow-slit model, the largest usable order for this positive wavelength separation must satisfy (m+1/N)λ1​≤d. Since d/λ1​=125, this permits m≤124, giving the formal all-order result
Δλmin,124​=0.516nm.​
(15)
That pair meets the criterion at θ≃83.1∘. Order 125 of λ1​ is at grazing incidence and the corresponding longer-wavelength peak cannot propagate. In a real device, finite slit width, weak high-order intensity and screen acceptance may prevent such an extreme order from being used; those data are absent. Thus the specified-order expression, and 64nm when first order is intended, are the defensible resolution answers under the stated criterion.

5 OurBigBook.com
For a photon, the photon energy formula and the vacuum relation ν=c/λ give Eγ​=hc/λ. For an electron, the de Broglie wavelength gives the same momentum magnitude p=h/λ, but the nonrelativistic kinetic energy is Ke​=p2/(2me​). Using h=6.62607015×10−34Js, me​=9.10938×10−31kg and 1eV=1.602176634×10−19J,
Eγ​=4.0×10−9(6.62607015×10−34)(2.99792458×108)​=4.96611×10−17J,
(16)
Ke​=2(9.10938×10−31)(4.0×10−9)2(6.62607015×10−34)2​=1.50617×10−20J.
(17)
Thus, to the precision of the wavelength,
Eγ​=3.1×102eV,Ke​=9.4×10−2eV.​
(18)
The electron answer is its kinetic energy, as required for the diffraction experiment; its relativistic energy would additionally include the approximately 511keV rest energy. Since Ke​≪me​c2, the nonrelativistic approximation is well justified. Equal wavelengths imply equal momenta, not equal energies for particles with different energy–momentum relations.

Put the charged sheet at z=0 and the grounded plates at z=±d/2. By symmetry the electric field points away from the positive sheet with equal magnitude in the two gaps. A Gaussian pillbox crossing the sheet gives
Ez​(0+)−Ez​(0−)=ε0​σ​,∣E∣=2ε0​σ​.
(19)
The plate boundary conditions fix their electric potentials to zero. For the charged sheet between grounded parallel plates, the central potential is
Vs​=∣E∣2d​=4ε0​σd​,σ=1.0×10−7Cm−2,d=1.0×10−2m.
(20)
With vacuum permittivity ε0​=8.85419×10−12Fm−1, Vs​≃28.24V. An electron has electric charge −e, so moving from a grounded plate to this positive potential decreases its potential energy by eVs​. Conservation of energy then gives
21​me​v2=eVs​=4ε0​eσd​,v=2ε0​me​eσd​​≃3.2×106ms−1.​
(21)
The unrounded value is 3.15×106ms−1, about 0.0105c. Either plate gives the same speed. The ideal calculation neglects the electron's disturbance of the prescribed field and image-force effects at its release point, consistently with treating it as a test particle.

Powered vertical flight. Take upward velocity v as positive, and let ve​>0 be the downward exhaust speed relative to the rocket. During dt the rocket's mass changes by dm<0, and exhaust mass −dm leaves with Earth-frame velocity v−ve​. Compare the momentum of the rocket plus this newly expelled exhaust before and after the interval:
(m+dm)(v+dv)+(−dm)(v−ve​)−mv=−mgdt.
(22)
Discard the second-order product dmdv. The result is mdv+ve​dm=−mgdt, or
mdtdv​=−ve​dtdm​−mg.
(23)
The positive rocket thrust is −ve​m˙. Integrating with v(0)=0 and m(0)=m0​ gives the rocket equation with gravitational loss:
v(t)=ve​lnm(t)m0​​−gt.​
(24)
Using d(mv)/dt for the rocket alone without the exhaust momentum flux would give the wrong equation for this open system.
Orbital speed under the stated gravity assumption. A circular orbit of radius ro​=RE​+ho​=7.90×106m requires centripetal acceleration vo2​/ro​. If the magnitude of gravitational acceleration is the stipulated constant g=9.8ms−2 even at the orbit,
ro​vo2​​=g,vo​=gro​​=8.80×103ms−1.​
(25)
This treats gravity as centrally directed for the orbital calculation, while retaining its constant magnitude. The subsequent flat-surface approximation treats its direction as locally vertical.
Burnout height. During the unpowered projectile motion, horizontal velocity is constant. At the top of the trajectory the vertical component vanishes, so the horizontal component must equal the orbital speed vo​. At burnout, therefore,
vy,b​=vo​tan30∘,ho​−hb​=2gvy,b2​​=6gvo2​​.
(26)
These follow either by integrating y¨​=−g or by the vertical work-energy theorem. Substituting the preceding constant-g orbital result gives
hb​=ho​−6RE​+ho​​=1.83×105m≃183km.​
(27)
The vertical component is initially positive, as required to reach the orbit after burnout.
Alternative inverse-square interpretation. A real Earth's exterior Newtonian gravitational field is not constant over a 1500km altitude change. If 9.8ms−2 instead means the surface value g0​, then Newton's law of universal gravitation gives GM=g0​RE2​ and
vo​=RE​+ho​g0​RE2​​​=7.13×103ms−1.
(28)
Using this orbital speed but the paper's constant-g flat projectile motion approximation for the coast would give
hb​=1.50×106−6(RE​+ho​)RE2​​=6.36×105m≃636km.​
(29)
This alternative changes the global constant-gravity assumption; it is not the same model as the 183km result. An exact curved Kepler orbit coast would also abandon the prescribed flat trajectory. The printed assumptions support the constant-magnitude answers above, while the inverse-square values explain the different answer obtained from the usual physical Earth-orbit formula.

Directions. Choose +x along the horizontal spindle from the pivot to the disk, and +z vertically upward. With lever arm r=lx and weight Fg​=−mgz, the torque about the pivot is
τ=r×Fg​=mgly​.
(30)
Clockwise precession viewed from above has Ω=−Ωz. The relation τ=Ω×L therefore requires the spin angular momentum to point along −x, from the disk toward the pivot. The disk spins clockwise when viewed from its outer face looking along the spindle toward the pivot. Looking from the pivot reverses that apparent rotation. The right-hand rule fixes these signs unambiguously.
The drawing shows an instantaneous top view; the disk's angular momentum and the horizontal spindle turn clockwise together. The pivot force has zero torque about the pivot.
Rate of precession. For steady horizontal motion the spin contribution has magnitude L=Iω and turns through dϕ=Ωdt in time dt. Its change is perpendicular to itself and has magnitude dL=Ldϕ. Hence
∣τ∣=​dtdL​​=ΩIω=mgl,Ω=Iωmgl​.​
(31)
This is the usual slow steady gyroscope precession relation. Any constant vertical angular momentum associated with steady precession has zero time derivative; the horizontal spin contribution supplies the changing component here. Transient nutation is excluded by the prescribed horizontal steady motion.
Clock design. Convert both rotation rates to angular frequencies:
Ω=602π​rads−1,ω=2π(300)rads−1.
(32)
For the moment of inertia of a uniform disc, I=mR2/2, so the mass cancels:
l=2gΩR2ω​=2(9.8)(2π/60)(0.10)2(600π)​=0.1007m≃10.1cm.​
(33)
Spin friction. At fixed geometry, reducing ω increases Ω∝1/ω. The precession period, Tp​=2π/Ω, therefore decreases. This trend holds while slow steady precession remains a suitable description; it cannot be extrapolated to a stopped disk.
Counterweight. To oppose the disk's gravitational torque, place the counterweight on the other side of the pivot, at −lc​x. The net torque is
τ=g(ml−mc​lc​)y​.
(34)
A horizontal axle can remain fixed when this vanishes, giving
lc​=mc​ml​on the opposite side of the pivot.​
(35)
For the fixed spin direction already found, counterbalanced gyroscope precession has signed rate
Ωz​=−Iωg(ml−mc​lc​)​.
(36)
Moving the counterweight outward from the pivot first slows the clockwise motion, eliminates its driving torque at balance, and then reverses the steady motion to counterclockwise. A counterweight on the disk's side would add to the gravitational torque. These statements neglect axial spin moment of inertia of the counterweight and assume the stated horizontal motion, without a separately imposed precession at balance.

9 OurBigBook.com
Momentum identity. From the Lorentz factor, v2/c2=1−γ−2. The relativistic three-momentum therefore satisfies
p2=γ2m2v2=m2c2γ2(1−γ−2),p2=m2c2(γ2−1).​
(37)
Together with relativistic energy E=γmc2, this gives the energy–momentum relation E2−p2c2=m2c4.
Parent in the laboratory. The rest energy is m0​c2=1GeV, while the total relativistic energy is 3GeV. Consequently
γ0​=3,cv0​​=1−91​​=38​​=0.942809.​
(38)
Its momentum magnitude is p0​c=32−12​GeV=8​GeV.
Daughters in the zero-momentum frame. The centre-of-momentum frame is initially the parent's rest frame. Conservation of momentum gives p1∗​=−p2∗​. Equal daughter rest masses then imply equal relativistic energies. Conservation of relativistic energy gives
EX∗​=2m0​c2​=21​GeV,γX​=mX​c2EX∗​​=m0​/3m0​/2​=23​.
(39)
Their speeds are therefore
γX​=23​,cvX∗​​=1−94​​=35​​=0.745356.​
(40)
The two velocities are opposite, and pX∗​c=(1/2)2−(1/3)2​GeV=5​GeV/6. Their total kinetic energy is m0​c2−2mX​c2=m0​c2/3.
Invariant of the complete system. Before the decay, in the centre-of-momentum frame,
Ibefore​=(m0​c2)2−0=m02​c4.
(41)
After the relativistic two-body decay,
Iafter​=(EX∗​+EX∗​)2−c2∣pX∗​+(−pX∗​)∣2=(m0​c2)2.
(42)
In the laboratory, four-momentum conservation fixes the summed daughter energy to 3GeV and their summed momentum to the parent's p0​. Thus the same calculation is
Ibefore​=Iafter​=(3GeV)2−(8​GeV)2=1GeV2=m02​c4.​
(43)
The invariant is formed after summing the daughter four-momenta; adding their separate squared rest energies would omit the relative-motion contribution to the invariant mass of the pair.

Axial moment of inertia. In the original diagram R1​ is the outer radius and R2​ the inner radius. For uniform mass density ρ, a coaxial annulus of thickness dr has dm=2πρLrdr. Therefore the axial moment of inertia of a hollow cylinder is
I=∫R2​R1​​r2dm=2πρL∫R2​R1​​r3dr=2πρL​(R14​−R24​).
(44)
Since M=πρL(R12​−R22​), factorizing the fourth-power difference gives
I=21​M(R12​+R22​).​
(45)
For a solid cylinder R2​→0, giving I=MR12​/2. For a thin cylindrical shell with fixed mass and R1​,R2​→R, I=MR2. The latter limit agrees with every mass element being at radius R.
Undamped rolling oscillations. Let x be axle displacement from the spring equilibrium. Rolling without slipping imposes ∣ωroll​∣=∣x˙∣/R. The sum of translational and rotational kinetic energy is
T=21​mx˙2+21​IR2x˙2​=21​(m+R2I​)x˙2.
(46)
The potential energy is U=kx2/2. Differentiating T+U in the absence of damping, or applying the force and torque equations below, gives
(m+R2I​)x¨+kx=0.
(47)
For the thin shell I=mR2, the effective inertia is 2m, and the angular frequency of the simple harmonic motion is
ω0​=2mk​​.​
(48)
Static contact friction supplies the required torque but does no work when the contact point is instantaneously stationary.
Damped force balance. Take rightward force as positive and counterclockwise rotation as positive. Write f for the signed static friction at the bottom contact. Then
mx¨=−kx−bx˙+f,Iα=fR,α=−Rx¨​.
(49)
Eliminate f=−Ix¨/R2 and use I=mR2:
2mx¨+bx˙+kx=0,x¨+Bx˙+Cx=0,B=2mb​,C=2mk​.​
(50)
Here b has units kgs−1, so B has units s−1 and C units s−2. The stated drag force is interpreted as acting through the axle, with no additional viscous torque. An oil bath could also exert such a torque physically, but its magnitude is not specified by this force-only model.
Light damping. Substitution of z=Ae−pt into the differential equation gives p2−Bp+C=0. In the underdamped regime B2<4C,
p=2B​±iC−4B2​​=4mb​±iωd​,ωd​=2mk​−16m2b2​​.
(51)
Taking real linear combinations gives the general damped harmonic oscillator displacement
x(t)=e−bt/(4m)[A1​cos(ωd​t)+A2​sin(ωd​t)].​
(52)
The constants are fixed by the initial displacement and velocity. For example, release from rest at x0​ gives A1​=x0​ and A2​=bx0​/(4mωd​). Light damping means b2≪8mk, in which case ωd​≃ω0​ and the envelope decays slowly compared with an oscillation.

Complex impedance. In sinusoidal steady state write physical voltage and electric current as real parts of Veiωt and Ieiωt. The electrical impedance Z=V/I is a ratio of phasors; its magnitude gives the voltage-to-current amplitude ratio and its argument gives their phase difference. It is measured in ohms.
For an ideal capacitor, q=Cv and i=dq/dt=Cdv/dt. Consequently I=iωCV, giving
ZC​=iωC1​=−ωCi​.​
(53)
With this time convention the voltage lags the electric current by π/2.
Bridge output. The original diagram has R1​ and C1​ in parallel in the upper-left arm, and R2​ and C2​ in series in the lower-left arm. The point labelled C is connected to the upper supply node. Set the lower supply node to zero, so VC​=Vi​. Assuming the measured output draws negligible electric current, the two voltage dividers give
VA​=Vi​Z1​+Z2​Z2​​,VB​=Vi​R3​+R4​R4​​.
(54)
Their difference is therefore
Vi​VAB​​=Z1​+Z2​Z2​​−R3​+R4​R4​​.​
(55)
The reactive-arm electrical impedances are
Z1​=(R1​1​+iωC1​)−1,Z2​=R2​+iωC2​1​.
(56)
Balance. Setting VAB​=0 and cross-multiplying gives R3​Z2​=R4​Z1​. For this Wien bridge,
Z1​Z2​​=(R2​+iωC2​1​)(R1​1​+iωC1​)=R1​R2​​+C2​C1​​+i(ωR2​C1​−ωR1​C2​1​).
(57)
The right-hand side must be the real number R4​/R3​. Equating imaginary and real parts gives
ω=R1​R2​C1​C2​​1​,C2​C1​​=R3​R4​​−R1​R2​​.​
(58)
Positive capacitances require R4​/R3​>R2​/R1​. In the equal-component case R1​=R2​=R and C1​=C2​=C, this reduces to
ω=RC1​,R4​=2R3​.​
(59)
Band-pass output and phase. Preserve the requested voltage polarity: VAC​=VA​−VC​. Since VC​=Vi​,
Vi​VAC​​=Z1​+Z2​Z2​​−1=−Z1​+Z2​Z1​​.
(60)
Put u=ωRC>0. The equal-component ratio is Z2​/Z1​=2+i(u−u−1), so the Wien bridge band-pass response is
H(ω)=Vi​VAC​​=−3+i(u−u−1)1​=−1−u2+3iuiu​.​
(61)
At finite positive frequency, its imaginary part vanishes exactly when u−u−1=0. Thus
ωr​=RC1​,H(ωr​)=−31​.​
(62)
The magnitude ∣H∣=[9+(u−u−1)2]−1/2 is maximal there and tends to zero at both frequency extremes, as expected for a band-pass filter.
A convenient continuous, unwrapped wave phase is
ϕ(ω)=−π−arctan(3u−u−1​).​
(63)
It decreases from −π/2 as ω→0+, passes through −π at ωr​, and tends to −3π/2 as ω→∞. A principal-value plot instead jumps from −π to +π at resonance; both represent the same phasor. Reversing the output to VCA​ would shift the phase by π and make the resonant ratio +1/3, but that is a different output polarity from the one printed.

12 OurBigBook.com
Reflection and central spot. At a boundary from lower to higher refractive index, the near-normal electric-field reflection coefficient is negative, r=(n1​−n2​)/(n1​+n2​). This gives a π wave phase reversal on reflection from the glass plate through the air film. Reflection at the lens's glass-to-air underside has no such reversal. These are consequences of the Fresnel equations for the reflected electric field.
At ideal contact the film thickness is zero, so the two reflected contributions have zero geometrical optical path difference but a relative π phase reversal. They produce destructive interference, and the central spot is dark. This conclusion concerns the film reflection; other lens surfaces can add a weak background.
Rings and their radii. At radial distance r, let the air thickness be t. The two relevant rays reflect at the upper and lower film interfaces. The lower reflection accumulates an extra round-trip optical path length 2t, plus the relative π reflection shift. As t increases away from contact, alternating constructive and destructive thin-film interference forms Newton's rings. At near-normal incidence, a bright ring satisfies
λ2π​(2t)+π=2π(m+1),2t=(m+21​)λ,m=0,1,2,….
(64)
The extended source can illuminate these localized film fringes: each incident contribution interferes with its own two reflected paths; unrelated source points need not be mutually coherent.
For the spherical lens surface, geometry gives r2+(R−t)2=R2, so r2=2Rt−t2. Since t≪R, t≃r2/(2R). Combining the equations yields
rm​=Rλ(m+21​)​.​
(65)
The m=0 bright ring is the first bright ring around the dark contact point.
Curvature from ring diameters. Writing Dm​=2rm​, subtract the squared diameters to eliminate the unknown initial order:
Dm+202​−Dm2​=4Rλ(20).
(66)
Using SI units,
R=80(500×10−9)(7.1×10−3)2−(3.3×10−3)2​=0.988m≃0.99m.​
(67)
Liquid-filled film. With film refractive index n=1.4, still smaller than both glass indices, there remains exactly one relative reflection phase reversal. The round-trip optical path length is now 2nt, so
rm2​=nRλ​(m+21​).
(68)
Here λ=500nm is the illuminating vacuum wavelength, approximately its air value, rather than its shorter value inside the liquid. The ring labelled m=2 therefore has diameter
D2​=21.4(0.988)(500×10−9)(2+1/2)​​=1.878×10−3m≃1.9mm.​
(69)
Filling the gap contracts each ring radius by 1/n​ at fixed order and curvature.

Equation and interpretation. The supplied equation is the time-independent Schrödinger equation for a nonrelativistic particle with mass m in a prescribed potential energy V(x). Equivalently,
Hψ=Eψ,H=−2mℏ2​dx2d2​+V(x).
(70)
It is an eigenvalue problem for the Hamiltonian operator. A stationary energy state has full wavefunction Ψ(x,t)=ψ(x)e−iEt/ℏ. By the Born rule, ∣ψ(x)∣2dx is the probability of finding the particle in a small interval dx, with wavefunction normalization ∫−∞∞​∣ψ∣2dx=1.
Infinite barriers. Infinite exterior potential energy excludes any finite-energy probability outside the interval. The infinite square well consequently has ψ=0 outside and the hard-wall boundary conditions
ψ(0)=ψ(a)=0.​
(71)
The interior wavefunction must meet the zero exterior amplitude continuously. Its derivative need not be continuous across an infinite wall; imposing both zero value and zero derivative would eliminate every nonzero interior solution.
Ground state. Inside the well V=0, so ψ′′+k2ψ=0, with k=2mE​/ℏ. Its general solution is Asinkx+Bcoskx. The left wall gives B=0, and the right wall gives ka=nπ for n=1,2,…. Thus the discrete energy eigenvalues are En​=n2π2ℏ2/(2ma2). The smallest, n=1, is the ground state. Since
∫0a​sin2aπx​dx=2a​,
(72)
its normalized wavefunction, choosing an irrelevant overall phase to make it positive inside, is
ψ1​(x)={2/a​sin(πx/a),0,​0<x<a,x≤0 or x≥a,​E1​=2ma2π2ℏ2​.​
(73)
Finite barriers. For a finite step and constant particle mass, both ψ and ψ′ are continuous at x=0,a. Wavefunction matching at a finite potential step follows by integrating the Schrödinger equation across a vanishingly small neighborhood of the step: a bounded potential cannot generate a finite jump in ψ′. The bound-state exterior solutions decay rather than vanish identically:
ψ(x)∝eκx(x<0),ψ(x)∝e−κ(x−a)(x>a),κ=ℏ2m(Vw​−E)​​.
(74)
Normalizability excludes the growing exterior exponentials. The equivalent interior boundary conditions are ψ′(0)=κψ(0) and ψ′(a)=−κψ(a); neither boundary value is zero for the nontrivial ground state.
The ground state of a finite square well remains symmetric about a/2 and has no nodes. It bends smoothly into exponential tails at both walls, extending over a larger region than the infinite-well state. Its maximum after normalization is lower for the deep well considered here. When Vw​≫E, the penetration length 1/κ is short, so the two shapes are close except near the walls and in the exterior tails.
The finite curve is an illustrative exact matched solution with Vw​=10E1,∞​; no numerical wall height is specified by the question.
Energy comparison. The finite barriers relax the confinement, allowing a less rapidly varying interior wavefunction and therefore smaller kinetic energy. More explicitly, the even interior solution is proportional to cos[k(x−a/2)], and matching to the tails gives ktan(ka/2)=κ. The lowest root lies at 0<ka<π, while the infinite well has ka=π. Hence
E1,finite​<2ma2π2ℏ2​=E1,∞​.​
(75)
As Vw​→∞, the tails disappear and the finite-well energy approaches the infinite-well value from below. This comparison uses the same zero of potential energy inside both wells.

Field of discrete masses. Newton's law of universal gravitation and superposition give the gravitational field away from the source points:
g(r)=−Gi=1∑N​Mi​∣r−ri​∣3r−ri​​.​
(76)
It is the force per unit test mass, with units Nkg−1=ms−2, and points toward each positive source mass.
Infinite circular cylindrical rod. Let b be the radius of the circular cross-section, so A=πb2, and write λ=ρA for the linear mass density. Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface with radius r>b and length L. Translation and rotation symmetry make g=gr​(r)r. The end caps have zero field flux because their normals are axial; on the curved surface the outward-normal component is the constant negative value gr​. Gauss's law for gravity therefore gives
∮g⋅dS=2πrLgr​=−4πG(ρAL),g(r)=−r2GρA​r(r>b).​
(77)
The gravitational field of an infinite uniform cylinder inside the material instead has enclosed mass ρπr2L, giving gr​=−2πGρr. The exterior result assumes a circular cylindrical rod; area by itself would not specify the exact near field of a noncircular cross-section.
In the left panel the dashed circle is a transverse section of the coaxial Gaussian surface; the field points inward and the surface normals outward. Its side area is 2πrL.
For an exterior circular orbit, Newton's second law equates the force required for centripetal acceleration to gravity:
rmv2​=mr2GρA​,v=2GρA​=2Gλ​.​
(78)
The orbital speed is independent of radius and of the orbiting object's mass, for orbits outside the infinite rod.
Finite rod. Taking the supplied field as the gravitational field of a finite uniform line segment, the corresponding balance at radius R is
Rv2​=RR2+a2​GM​,v(R)=(R2+a2​GM​)1/2=(R2+a2)1/4GM​​.​
(79)
Since M=2aρA=2aλ, its two limits are
R≪a:v≃aGM​​=2GρA​,R≫a:v≃RGM​​.​
(80)
The first reproduces the infinite-rod result: a nearby observer sees a very long source. The second is the familiar circular orbit speed about a point mass, since a distant observer cannot resolve the rod's length. The dimensionless curve is
GM/a​v​=[1+(R/a)2]−1/4.
(81)
It starts at a constant plateau and decreases smoothly, approaching an R−1/2 dependence far away. For R>0, dv/dR=−GM​R/[2(R2+a2)5/4]<0, consistent with the sketch.
Derivation of the finite-rod field. Put the source along −a<z<a on the z axis. In its central perpendicular plane, an element dm=λdz is at distance s=r2+z2​. Its field magnitude is Gλdz/s2, and its inward radial component has the extra factor r/s. The axial components cancel between z and −z. Thus
gr​=−Gλr∫−aa​(r2+z2)3/2dz​=−Gλr[r2r2+z2​z​]−aa​=−rr2+a2​2aGλ​.
(82)
Replacing 2aλ by M gives
g(r)=−rr2+a2​GM​r.​
(83)
The integral treats the source as a line mass. For a finite cylinder of nonzero cross-section, the displayed finite-rod formula is a thin-rod approximation, not an exact field for all r. Its near-rod limit should therefore be read as b≪R≪a, keeping the orbit outside the material; the apparent line-source singularity at r=0 does not describe the interior of a real cylinder.

a OurBigBook.com
An electric dipole is a localized pair of opposite electric charges, or more generally a neutral electric charge distribution with nonzero first electric moment. For charges −q and +q separated by displacement d directed from negative to positive, the electric dipole moment is
p=qd,[p]=Cm.​
(84)
A neutral molecule can have a permanent electric dipole moment when its positive and negative charge centres do not coincide. An applied electric field can also produce an induced electric dipole moment by distorting an initially nonpolar electric charge distribution.
At distance r≫∣d∣ in vacuum, expand the difference of the two point-charge potentials to first order in the separation. The leading electric potential is
Φ(r)=4πε0​r2p⋅r​.
(85)
The monopole term cancels because the net electric charge is zero. Taking E=−∇Φ gives the electric dipole field
E(r)=4πε0​r33(p⋅r)r−p​.​
(86)
On the dipole axis its magnitude is 2p/(4πε0​r3) and its direction is along p; in the equatorial plane the magnitude is p/(4πε0​r3) and the field points opposite to p. The r−3 decay is faster than the r−2 field of an isolated point charge.
In a uniform external electric field, the opposite forces on the two charges cancel in their resultant but form a couple. Its torque is
τ=p×E,∣τ∣=pEsinθ.
(87)
For a fixed permanent electric dipole moment, the interaction potential energy is
U=−p⋅E=−pEcosθ.​
(88)
Differentiating with respect to orientation recovers the torque. Parallel alignment minimizes U and is stable against a small rotation; antiparallel alignment maximizes U and is unstable. Rotating a fixed dipole slowly from parallel to antiparallel requires external work 2pE.
A nonuniform electrostatic electric field can also exert a net force. Expanding the two charge forces gives F≃(p⋅∇)E, which equals ∇(p⋅E) for a fixed dipole in a curl-free electrostatic field. Thus a suitably aligned dipole is attracted toward stronger field. An induced electric dipole moment requires care in computing energy: when p=αE for constant isotropic electric polarizability, building the dipole costs energy and the effective interaction is U=−αE2/2, rather than substituting directly into the fixed-dipole formula. These field, torque and energy effects explain molecular orientation and electric polarization.

b OurBigBook.com
A conservative vector field has path-independent work: the integral ∫AB​F⋅dr depends only on its endpoints. Equivalently, the line integral around every closed path in its domain vanishes. One can then define a single-valued potential energy U by
U(B)−U(A)=−∫AB​F⋅dr,F=−∇U,WA→B​=U(A)−U(B).​
(89)
The arbitrary additive constant in U has no effect on the force. A useful zero is often chosen at infinity for a localized attractive interaction.
A differentiable conservative force has ∇×F=0 because the curl of a gradient vanishes. Conversely, a smooth curl-free field on a simply connected domain admits a global scalar potential. The domain condition matters: on the punctured plane, F=(C/r)θ has zero curl away from the missing origin but closed-loop work 2πC around it. It is not globally conservative there. The existence of a local potential does not establish a single-valued potential throughout a domain with holes.
The work-energy theorem gives ΔT=W for kinetic energy T. If all forces are conservative and U has no explicit time dependence, then
ΔT=−ΔU,T+U=constant.​
(90)
This is conservation of mechanical energy. In one dimension, an equilibrium occurs at dU/dx=0; a local minimum with U′′>0 is stable, while a maximum with U′′<0 is unstable. Expanding about a minimum gives U≃U0​+U′′(x0​)(x−x0​)2/2, producing simple harmonic motion with ω2=U′′(x0​)/m.
Examples include the spring force Fx​=−kx with U=kx2/2, the near-surface gravitational force −mgz with U=mgz, and the central Newtonian gravitational field with U=−GMm/r. An electrostatic force on a fixed electric charge q has U=qΦ, where Φ is the electric potential.
Sliding friction provides a contrasting physical test: traversing a closed path still dissipates mechanical energy, since the frictional force opposes the local motion on both outward and return legs. Its work depends on path length and cannot be represented by a position-only U. Total energy can remain conserved when the resulting internal energy is included. Also, even if F=−∇U(r,t) at each instant, explicit time dependence gives d(T+U)/dt=∂U/∂t; a static conservative-field argument alone does not guarantee constant mechanical energy in that situation.

c OurBigBook.com
Faraday's law of induction relates an induced electromotive force to the rate of change of magnetic flux. Choose a positive orientation around a loop and its associated surface normal by the right-hand rule. For a stationary conducting loop,
ΦB​=∫S​B⋅dS,E=∮E⋅dl=−dtdΦB​​.​
(91)
Unlike an electrostatic field, the induced electric field generally has nonzero curl; the differential form is ∇×E=−∂B/∂t. For a moving circuit, magnetic flux transport for a moving circuit includes the magnetic Lorentz force on the charges:
E=∮(E+u×B)⋅dl=−dtdΦB​​,
(92)
where u is the local wire velocity. Thus changing the field or moving a conductor can produce induction.
The minus sign is Lenz's law: an induced electric current, when a closed conducting path permits it, produces a magnetic field opposing the change of linked flux. It need not oppose the original field itself. For example, increasing flux through a loop produces a current tending to reduce that increase; decreasing the same flux reverses the current. The opposition is consistent with conservation of energy: external mechanical or electrical work is needed to maintain a change against its inductive reaction.
For a coil of N turns, define the magnetic flux linkage Λ=∑j=1N​Φj​, reducing to NΦB​ when every turn links the same flux. For fixed geometry and a linear magnetic response, self-inductance L is defined by Λ=LI, and the coil's induced electromotive force is
Eself​=−LdtdI​,[L]=H=WbA−1.​
(93)
The corresponding terminal voltage drop, with the passive sign convention, is VL​=LdI/dt. It opposes changes in electric current; it does not require the current itself to vanish.
Building the current from zero requires power P=IVL​=LIdI/dt. Integrating gives the energy stored by an ideal inductor:
UB​=∫0I​LI′dI′=21​LI2.​
(94)
This energy is stored in the magnetic field and can be returned when the current falls. In a series RL circuit driven by a constant voltage V0​, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives LI˙+RI=V0​. Starting with zero current, I=(V0​/R)(1−e−tR/L), with time constant L/R. This makes the resistance to rapid current changes directly observable. Two coils also have mutual inductance: changing primary current induces secondary electromotive force −MdI1​/dt with a polarity determined by the chosen winding orientations, the principle behind a transformer.

d OurBigBook.com
For a light test particle of mass m outside a spherical source of mass M, Newton's law of universal gravitation gives F=−GMmr/r2. It is a central force, so its torque about the source vanishes and angular momentum L=mr×v is conserved. The motion therefore lies in a fixed plane when L=0. Its gravitational potential energy is −GMm/r, and conservation of mechanical energy gives
ϵ=2v2​−rGM​=constant,h=mL​=∣r×v∣=constant.
(95)
Here ϵ is specific orbital energy and h is specific angular momentum. A Kepler orbit has polar equation
r(θ)=1+ecosθp​,p=GMh2​,e2=1+(GM)22ϵh2​.​
(96)
The angle is measured from periapsis. The conic section is an ellipse for ϵ<0 and 0≤e<1, a parabola for ϵ=0 and e=1, and a hyperbola for ϵ>0 and e>1. The circle is the e=0 elliptical case. The special case h=0 is radial motion and must be handled as a degenerate limit. Bound ellipses have the source at one focus, which is Kepler's first law.
For a bound orbit of semi-major axis a, ϵ=−GM/(2a). Combining this with the energy equation gives the vis-viva equation:
v2=GM(r2​−a1​).​
(97)
The particle therefore moves faster near periapsis and slower near apoapsis. Conservation of angular momentum also gives constant areal velocity, dA/dt=h/2, expressing Kepler's second law. Using the ellipse's area and h2=GMa(1−e2) gives the orbital period
T2=GM4π2a3​,​
(98)
which is Kepler's third law.
A circular orbit follows from centripetal acceleration vc2​/r=GM/r2, giving vc​=GM/r​ and T=2πr3/(GM)​. The minimum escape velocity from radius r follows from the marginally unbound condition ϵ=0:
vc​=rGM​​,vesc​=r2GM​​=2​vc​.​
(99)
These ideal orbits neglect drag force, other gravitating bodies and changes in the central source. For two comparable masses, the relative two-body problem uses G(M+m) instead of GM. An orbiting object is continuously in free fall; the inward gravitational force changes its direction even when its speed is constant. These inverse-square results assume the physical variation of gravity with radius, rather than extending a near-surface constant-g approximation to an entire orbit.
